title: English Language & Literature MYP 5 eAssessment-style Practice Paper 1

questions.content:
Text A (an extract from a short story, written for this paper)

The last bus out of Halden Street was always late, and tonight the shelter smelled of wet concrete and chip fat. Imani pulled her sleeves over her knuckles and counted the ticking of the streetlamp. Eleven minutes since the timetable said it should have come. Her phone, at four per cent, glowed like a small, tired moon in her palm.

Across the road, a man was dragging shutters down over the window of the fish bar, one slow rattle after another. He glanced at her, then at the dark, then away. She told herself that was kindness: the way people look at a stranger and decide not to make it their problem.

She had practised the sentence all week. Dad, I'm not going to be a doctor. Short. Clean. No apology in it. But on the walk from the audition hall the words had gone soft, like bread in rain, and now she could not remember how the sentence began.

The bus swung round the corner at last, brakes sighing, its windows a long yellow ribbon of light. Imani stood. The doors folded open. For a second she did not step on. Somewhere in her bag, wrapped in a school jumper, her trumpet case clicked as if it were breathing.

'You getting on, love?' the driver asked.

She nodded, and the doors closed behind her like a held breath finally let go.

Read Text A and answer the questions.

(a) Identify two details from the first paragraph that suggest the bus stop is an unwelcoming place. (2 marks)

(b) Explain what the writer suggests about how Imani feels about speaking to her father. (2 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a)
[1] One relevant detail from the first paragraph, e.g. the shelter smells of wet concrete and chip fat; the bus is eleven minutes late; the phone is almost out of battery.
[1] A second, different relevant detail.
(b)
[1] A valid inference, e.g. she is anxious or afraid of his reaction because she has rehearsed the sentence all week.
[1] Supported by a reference or quotation, e.g. 'the words had gone soft, like bread in rain' shows her confidence has weakened; she cannot remember how the sentence began.
Accept other valid inferences supported by the text.

'You getting on, love?' the driver asked.

She nodded, and the doors closed behind her like a held breath finally let go.

Analyse how the writer uses language and structure in Text A to create tension and to show Imani's hesitation. (6 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] Identifies a feature of setting description (e.g. 'wet concrete', the ticking streetlamp, the late bus) that builds a gloomy, waiting atmosphere.
[1] Explains the effect of the simile 'glowed like a small, tired moon', e.g. fragility, isolation, time running out.
[1] Comments on the man at the fish bar and the ambiguous idea of 'kindness', suggesting the indifference of strangers and Imani's loneliness.
[1] Analyses the rehearsed sentence and short fragments ('Short. Clean.') contrasted with the simile 'like bread in rain' to show her determination turning to doubt.
[1] Comments on structure, e.g. the movement from outward description to inner thought and back to the arrival of the bus, delaying the moment of decision to build suspense.
[1] Analyses the ending (the trumpet case 'breathing', the 'held breath' simile) as ambiguous, suggesting relief or release; uses accurate terminology and supports points with quotations.
Accept other valid analysis supported by the text.

questions.content:
Text B (an opinion article, written for this paper)

LET THEM SLEEP

Every weekday morning, millions of teenagers are dragged from their beds in the dark, handed a bag the weight of a small child and told to be bright, alert and ready to learn. It is a ridiculous expectation, and we should be ashamed that we still hold it.

Science is not on the side of the early bell. Teenagers' body clocks naturally shift later, which means that a student who is awake at seven is, biologically, still in the middle of the night. Would we ask adults to sit an exam at four in the morning? Of course not. Yet that is, in effect, what we demand of fifteen-year-olds.

Critics will say that later starts would wreck family routines and bus timetables. Fair enough: change is inconvenient. But inconvenience is a small price compared with a generation of exhausted, anxious young people who are struggling to concentrate. Several schools that have tried a later start report fewer late arrivals and calmer corridors.

So here is my challenge to head teachers, councillors and parents alike: stop treating sleep as a luxury. Move the bell. Give young people the one thing they cannot revise their way into, and watch what they can do when they are finally awake.

Read Text B and answer the questions.

(a) Identify the writer's purpose and the audience the writer is mainly addressing. Support each with one piece of evidence from the text. (2 marks)

(b) Explain how the writer organises the article to persuade the reader. (4 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a)
[1] Purpose: to persuade or argue that school should start later, supported by evidence such as the imperative 'Move the bell'.
[1] Audience: decision-makers and adults such as head teachers, councillors and parents, supported by the direct address in the final paragraph.
(b)
[1] The headline and opening paragraph hook the reader with a vivid, exaggerated picture of teenagers dragged from bed and introduce the argument immediately.
[1] The second paragraph builds the case with a scientific claim and a rhetorical question that invites the reader to agree.
[1] The third paragraph anticipates the opposing view ('Critics will say') and answers it, which strengthens the argument.
[1] The final paragraph closes with a direct challenge and a series of commands, leaving the reader with a call to action.
Accept other valid points about structure and its persuasive effect.

questions.content:
Text C (a poem, written for this paper)

Kitchen Light

Nan's kitchen kept its own weather:
steam at the window, a kettle's slow sermon,
the radio muttering news to nobody.
She measured nothing. A fistful, a pinch,

a splash of this. Her hands just knew,
as rivers know the sea. I stood
on a chair to watch the dough turn over,
its soft skin rising like a patient tide.

Now the house is sold. The chair is gone.
I stand in my own cold kitchen with a book
of careful grams and the correct oven heat,
and nothing I make will taste of her.

Still, when the bread is done, the light
comes through the window, thick and gold,
and for a moment I am small and floury
and someone is humming in the next room.

Analyse how the poet presents the speaker's feelings about loss and memory in Text C. (6 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] Comments on the metaphor 'kept its own weather' and personification of the kitchen as a warm, alive place.
[1] Analyses sensory details (steam, the kettle's 'slow sermon', the radio 'muttering') to create comfort and familiarity.
[1] Explains the effect of the simile 'as rivers know the sea' and the tide image for the grandmother's natural, instinctive skill.
[1] Identifies the shift at 'Now', contrasting the 'cold' kitchen and 'careful grams' with her old way of cooking, to show the sense of loss.
[1] Comments on the blunt, end-stopped statement 'nothing I make will taste of her' as conveying grief.
[1] Analyses the final stanza (golden light, humming, 'small and floury') as a turn towards consolation, showing memory can bring comfort; uses accurate terminology.
Accept other valid analysis supported by the text.

questions.content:
Text D (a draft paragraph from a student's report for the school newsletter)

Last week the school choir went to a competition at the city hall. they was very nervous but there performance was good. The conductor, Mr Okoro said it was the best they had ever sang, and everyone was like totally amazed. We think that the choir is great and we will definately go again next year.

(a) Identify and correct two errors of grammar, spelling or punctuation in Text D. (2 marks)

(b) Rewrite the paragraph in a formal register suitable for a school newsletter, correcting its errors and improving its style. (4 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a)
[1] One error correctly identified and corrected, e.g. 'they was' becomes 'they were'; 'there performance' becomes 'their performance'; 'definately' becomes 'definitely'; 'sang' becomes 'sung'; the missing capital letter or comma after 'Okoro'.
[1] A second, different error correctly identified and corrected.
(b)
[1] Informal expressions are replaced with formal vocabulary, e.g. 'like totally amazed' becomes 'astonished'.
[1] Grammar, verb forms and spelling are accurate throughout.
[1] Punctuation is accurate, including the capital letter and commas around the name of the conductor.
[1] The rewrite keeps the original meaning, has a consistent formal tone and varies sentence structure or uses connectives.
Accept other valid errors and rewrites.

Compare how Text A and Text C present a character reflecting on an important moment in their life. (4 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] Identifies a valid similarity, e.g. both present a character at an emotional threshold, thinking about people who matter to them.
[1] Identifies a valid difference, e.g. Imani is anxious about an uncertain future, while the speaker in the poem looks back at a lost past.
[1] Compares a technique used in both, e.g. similes (bread in rain, a patient tide) or imagery of light (the yellow ribbon of the bus, the thick gold light).
[1] Uses comparative language and refers to evidence from both texts.
Accept other valid comparisons.

questions.content:
Write a speech of about 400 words to be delivered at your school assembly. In it, argue that students should be encouraged to follow their own passions rather than choose only 'safe' careers. You should aim to persuade both students and teachers. (12 marks)

You will be assessed on your purpose and audience awareness, the structure of your speech, your persuasive techniques and the accuracy and variety of your language.
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] The purpose is clear and sustained throughout: the speech argues a definite position.
[1] There is clear awareness of the audience of students and teachers, e.g. direct address with 'you' and 'we'.
[1] The register is appropriate for a spoken school assembly, formal but engaging.
[1] The opening is engaging, e.g. a question, anecdote or striking statement.
[1] The central argument is clear and easy to follow.
[1] Ideas are developed with relevant examples, reasons or evidence.
[1] A range of persuasive techniques is used purposefully, e.g. rhetorical questions, the rule of three, repetition, emotive language.
[1] An opposing view is acknowledged and answered.
[1] The speech is organised logically into paragraphs with a clear progression of ideas.
[1] Connectives and linking devices create cohesion.
[1] Vocabulary and sentence structures are varied, and spelling, punctuation and grammar are mostly accurate.
[1] The conclusion is effective and ends with a memorable call to action.
Credit any valid approach that meets these qualities.
